Despite that, it is still a fun game. It does a good job of giving the player choices without the trite, binary decision events you see in many other games. I just finished the 1st episode (?... Season?... ?...) and I wanted to write a review since I have seen a negative review boil the game down to reading through a bunch of things and dragging pieces of text to a window. Yes. That's true; you do do that. However. In Orwell, you play the role of an investigator and as the story (yes there is a story, and, imho, a pretty well written one) unfolds into later chapters and becomes more complex, you as the investigator need to not only decide what information is important but also make judgement calls as to what piece of information is more correct (yes there are many times where information you come across is in conflict with another piece of information) when there is a discrepancy. There in lies the -real- beauty and, what I believe, to be the point of the game. I won't say more so as not to spoil it, but once you get to the end I think you'll see what I mean.

In any case, correctly unraveling the story requires you to learn about and know the characters involved as you need to also build a mental picture of who these people are and their social network (how they relate to one another). I would say it's definitely -not- a traditional game as the medium is click-drag and let go, but that's really more the medium than anything and a different experience is many times why people play a game by an indie studio; they are looking for a different experience.  And lets face it, people play visual novels (are they really even a game?). This game at least requires you to problem solve and critically think; there's even a deeper message behind it (again, no spoilers :) ).

The tl;dr is, yes it's click-drag, but it's real entertainment is in the story, the message behind it, the problem solving, the critical thinking, and making connections that don't immediately jump right out at you.

Currently very relevant and great simulated reality game with multiple possible endings. Several twists and turns in a story you have to uncover as an impartial outside "Investigator" hired to spy on (game world only) people for a neighboring country's secret government project called Orwell (named appropriately). This program that check's target's lives from personal blogs to professional and business internal calls is intended to make people safer, but some see it as a huge invasion of privacy. There's chat watching, e-mail reading, wiretapping, in-game-world internet research and more, where you make profiles of different characters and see their innocent or nefarious connections to one another and various organizations that may not be what they seem while gathering information about them to assess if they are a threat. Gripping, engaging story, with unique vector-style art and excellent music that seems perfect for all the "studying" you're doing for your "job."

I was intrigued by the game's title (specially being a fan of dystopian literature - I really appreciate Aldous Huxley and George Orwell's work) and decided to give it a try. I must say I was impressed both by the story and its intricacies but also by the technical aspects and design of this game. It is very simple, and that is precisely what made it so charming to my eyes.
In [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] you play as an investigator hired by [i]The Nation[/i], a country led by an authoritarian government named [i]The Party[/i], to work at [i]Orwell[/i], a covert surveillance system commissioned by the Ministry of Security through the Safety Bill. In the beginning you need to investigate a young woman with criminal history after a bomb goes off at the Freedom Plaza. Then, the story escalates. The main question this game presents is whether you'd sacrifice your freedom and privacy for "safety".
This game will run on any modern computer and I recommend it to any mature person who has 10€ to spare, specially if they have read and liked 1984. It is obviously not as intricate as the book, but it's very interesting nevertheless.
I have a negative remark to make about this game, though: [u]it is very slow[/u]. I personally read faster than the maximum text speed of this game and, specially when replaying to explore different options and get achievements, it put me off a little. Otherwise, I had a very pleasant experience.

If you liked [i]Orwell[/i], I would also recommend that you play [i]Headliner: Novinews[/i].

Verdict: 8/10

You play as an investigator for a government project called Orwell, which has been kicked into action after a bombing at a national monument. Your job is to use what's effectively GoogleGovernment to investigate suspects, finding how they're related to each other, and know as much about them as possible. The game has 3 endings I know of, and probably many more. The ending you get depends upon what information you place into Orwell. 

The game features a very unique and simple look, with low poly art for things such as images and the background, and what's effectively Internet Explorer and files displaying the information you have on suspects. The game's 'Internet Explorer' is used to discover information about people while on the other hand, the 'files section' shows all the information you placed into Orwell on a specific person, classed into categories, and people's relationships to one another.

Unfortunately, the game's does nothing when it comes to replaying, a concept I've only ever seen played off in Oxenfree, but 100% should be implemented in more games. After your first run, you know how the story twists and turns and can already account for it ahead of time. 

9.5/10 - It's well priced at $10, but if it's on sale, it's a must have.
